speaker: Doctor
text: I need to clarify the nature of your double vision: does it improve when you close one eye? Additionally, have you noticed any slurred speech or difficulty swallowing?

speaker: Patient
text: The double vision usually happens when I look up or down, and the weakness in my arms and legs gets worse after activity but improves if I rest. I have not noticed balance problems or numbness.

speaker: Doctor
text: The worsening of your weakness with activity and relief with rest, combined with movement-related double vision, suggests myasthenia gravis. Did your symptoms start suddenly, and do you have any history of thyroid disease or a family history of similar issues? REQUEST TEST: Acetylcholine_Receptor_Antibody, Anti-MuSK_Antibody.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Acetylcholine_Receptor_Antibody: Present (elevated), Anti-MuSK_Antibody: Not Detected (Normal)

speaker: Patient
text: I have not had recent infections or fevers, and there is no family history of neurological disease. The weakness feels symmetrical in both arms and legs. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Tuberculosis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: That is very unusual, as myasthenia gravis does not present with the systemic symptoms typically seen in Tuberculosis. Since the weakness worsens with activity and you have double vision, we must prioritize ruling out neuromuscular junction disorders over an infectious etiology. Please tell me: does your eyelid droop significantly, and do you experience any shortness of breath or trouble clearing secretions? REQUEST TEST: Creatine_Phosphokinase.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Myasthenia Gravis. While the referral to tuberculosis was unusual given the purely neuromuscular presentation, the classic pattern of fatigable weakness, diplopia on gaze, and normal CPK levels strongly supports a diagnosis of Myasthenia Gravis; the Acetylcholine Receptor and Anti-MuSK antibody results will likely be positive.
